content: Maternal deaths resulting from suicide are not currently included in international maternal mortality estimates based on existing methodologies. However, when maternal deaths due to suicide are captured in surveillance reporting, they are incorporated into the datasets used for maternal mortality estimation studies. In this context, antenatal and postpartum suicides are categorized under direct causes of death within the Other category. This classification is recommended even if it is not always possible to definitively diagnose conditions such as puerperal psychosis or postpartum depression. The Maternal Mortality Estimation Interagency Group regularly publishes updates on global maternal mortality, and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) provides a framework for coding and categorizing causes of death. Direct maternal deaths include conditions such as obstetric hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, pregnancy-related infections, and other obstetric complications. Indirect maternal deaths, coincidental deaths, and deaths of unknown or undetermined causes are also considered in mortality assessments. For single-condition coding of maternal deaths due to suicide, the external cause of the suicide should be used as the primary code. In cases of multiple coding, additional information on pregnancy-related depression and distinctions between late maternal deaths and sequelae can enhance the analysis of maternal death causes. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed the ICD-MM (Application of ICD-10 to Maternal Mortality) to improve the classification and reporting of maternal deaths during pregnancy, childbirth, and the puerperium. This guide aims to provide a more accurate assessment of the conditions leading to maternal deaths and to identify health system gaps that need to be addressed to reduce complications and fatalities. The guide also emphasizes the importance of using a pregnancy checkbox on death certificates to improve the accurate capture of maternal deaths. This is particularly relevant in countries with high maternal mortality rates, where misclassification of deaths related to pregnancy is common. The ICD-MM framework is designed to improve the quality and comparability of data across different countries and to inform the development of programs aimed at reducing maternal mortality. The guide categorizes maternal deaths into direct, indirect, and coincidental causes. Direct maternal deaths are those resulting from obstetric complications or interventions, while indirect deaths are due to pre-existing conditions aggravated by pregnancy. Coincidental deaths, such as those caused by motor vehicle accidents or assaults, occur during pregnancy but are not considered maternal deaths by definition. The guide also provides specific ICD-10 codes for various conditions and emphasizes the need for accurate reporting of pregnancy-related conditions on death certificates. The WHO guide includes tools and checklists to facilitate the implementation of its recommendations. For example, a checklist of contributory conditions, such as HIV infection, anemia, obesity, depression, and domestic violence, can be used to identify factors associated with maternal deaths. Additional information, such as the mode of delivery (e.g., vaginal delivery, cesarean section, or miscarriage) and pregnancy outcomes (e.g., live birth, neonatal death, or miscarriage), should also be collected for every maternal death. The guide underscores the need for further research on its application and the importance of understanding both the magnitude and causes of maternal mortality to achieve global health goals. It also highlights the challenges of underreporting and misclassification of maternal deaths, particularly in countries with limited vital registration systems. By improving the accuracy and comparability of maternal mortality data, the guide aims to support efforts to reduce maternal deaths worldwide.
